fun_facts: Despite the name, a little tunny isn't a true tuna: it belongs to a different genus, Euthynnus, and is more closely related to mackerel than to the yellowfin and blackfin tuna sharing the same water.

Anglers who catch one and expect table fare like its tuna cousins are usually disappointed: little tunny meat is dark and blood-rich, and unless it's bled and iced within minutes it turns strongly "fishy" fast, which is exactly why the species is nicknamed false albacore.
It's identified less by shape than by a scribble: a pattern of wavy, worm-like markings on its back above the lateral line, unlike any other fish sharing these waters.

measures.label: Fork length
measures.help: Measured along the curve of the body, from the tip of the upper jaw to the fork of the tail; curved fork length is the standard tuna-family measurement.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Little tunny cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward
